analysis.one_liner: Requires hotels and rental sites to show the full mandatory price upfront, not just at checkout.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill by voice vote on April 28, 2025; it has sat on the Senate calendar since April 29 with no vote taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill makes hotels, short-term rentals, and booking websites show the total price, including all mandatory service fees like resort fees, from the first moment a price appears — not just in the final checkout step. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general can enforce it. It took effect 450 days after any signing, and it preempts weaker state rules that don't require the same full-price display.
analysis.who_benefits: Travelers booking hotels and short-term rentals. Right now, a room advertised at $150 can quietly carry a $50-a-night mandatory 'resort fee' that only appears deep in the checkout process, making it hard to compare real prices across listings. Under the bill, every advertised price must include those mandatory fees upfront, so shoppers see the true cost before they pick a room and hotels that quote honest full prices no longer lose business to ones that hide fees.

how_it_helps.text: A covered entity — a hotel, short-term rental, third-party booking site, or comparison platform — cannot display or advertise a price that does not clearly and prominently show the total services price, including the base price plus every mandatory service fee [S3].

The full price must be disclosed when the services are first displayed and at every point afterward in the buying process, and any government taxes or fees must be disclosed before the final purchase [S3].

The rule covers the whole booking chain — hotels, short-term rentals, third-party online sellers, and intermediaries including metasearch referral sites — so a fee can't simply be pushed to whichever link in the chain doesn't have to show it [S3].

Enforcement runs through the Federal Trade Commission, which may treat violations as unfair or deceptive practices under its existing penalty framework, and through state attorneys general, who may sue on behalf of their residents [S3].
Hotels and short-term rentals that already advertise honest all-in prices get a level playing field, because competitors can no longer win clicks with a stripped-down base price [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Hotels and booking platforms that rely on mandatory add-on fees — resort fees, destination fees, cleaning fees — to advertise low headline prices, plus ordinary compliance costs of rebuilding price displays across websites and apps. Consumers, in principle, pay nothing; the mandatory fees were already being charged, the bill just forces them onto the first screen.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hotels and booking sites that hide fees

drawbacks.text: The displayed total is not truly all-in: taxes and government assessments only have to appear 'prior to the final purchase,' and optional add-ons are excluded entirely, so the number a shopper first sees can still be lower than what they eventually pay [S3].

The bill preempts state and local fee-disclosure rules unless those rules require the same total-services-price display, so states with stricter or differently designed disclosure laws would see them displaced by the federal floor [S3].

Third-party booking sites get an affirmative defense if they relied in good faith on inaccurate price information supplied by a hotel and fixed it after notice, which gives intermediaries a way to shift blame and slows correction of bad listings [S3].

A contract clause explicitly protects indemnification agreements between booking platforms and hotels over exchanged price information, a provision platforms sought to manage liability when a hotel's fee data is wrong [S3].
The prohibition does not take effect until 450 days after enactment, so hidden fees could continue through much of another booking season [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and everyday: travelers get the true mandatory price at first glance instead of at checkout, which is exactly the 'drip pricing' pattern the FTC has targeted. The costs fall on firms that must retool their displays, and the honest objection is that the bill's 'total price' still excludes taxes until the final step and excludes optional charges entirely, so it tames rather than eliminates the gap between advertised and final price. The preemption clause trades some state-level rules for a single national standard. On balance, a modest, well-aimed consumer rule with limited downside.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by voice vote under a fast-track procedure used for noncontroversial bills, and it has been sitting on the Senate's calendar of general orders ever since, waiting for the Senate to bring it up.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 21, 2025, by Rep. Young Kim (R-CA) and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee [S1][S5].

The committee considered and marked up the bill on April 8, 2025, and ordered it reported by voice vote; it was formally reported on April 24 with House Report 119-71 and placed on the Union Calendar [S5].

On April 28, 2025, the House took it up under 'suspension of the rules' — a fast-track process reserved for bills expected to face no opposition — and passed it by voice vote after forty minutes of debate [S5].

The Senate received the bill on April 29, 2025, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 60, where it has remained with no further action in the record [S5][S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, hotels and booking platforms that profit from advertising stripped-down prices keep the status quo while the bill waits on the Senate calendar; travelers keep seeing base prices without mandatory fees.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew cosponsors from both parties (4 Democrats, 2 Republicans), cleared committee and passed the House by voice vote with no recorded opposition, and no member or group is on record against it.

industries.industry: Hotels with mandatory resort and destination fees
industries.note: These hotels currently advertise a low base price and add a mandatory fee late in checkout; the bill forces the fee onto the first displayed price, weakening their main pricing tactic. Travelers can finally compare true prices across properties.

industries.industry: Online travel agencies and metasearch platforms (booking and comparison sites)
industries.note: Booking intermediaries must show the total price everywhere they display lodging, but the bill gives them an affirmative defense when a hotel supplies bad data, plus explicit protection for indemnification contracts between platforms and hotels. Their interest in keeping headline prices low runs against travelers' interest in seeing the full cost.

Short-term rentals (under 30 days) are covered like hotels, so cleaning and service fees must appear in the advertised total; many large platforms already display totals, so the adjustment is smaller for them than for traditional hotels.
State attorneys general gain a new federal cause of action to sue lodging firms on behalf of residents, alongside FTC enforcement.

analysis.trajectory: The bill passed the House by voice vote, so it faces no recorded opposition, but thousands of House-passed bills die each Congress waiting on the Senate calendar. Because it is short and noncontroversial, its realistic path to law is passage by unanimous consent or a short floor debate, which the Senate leadership could schedule at any time; without that, it will sit on Calendar No. 60 through the rest of the 119th Congress.
